snip.t: Skin-prick tests (SPT) should be performed in all cases.

faq.a: No; it shows sensitisation. Clinical correlation with history is required to confirm true allergy.
faq.q: Can a positive skin prick test guarantee that the patient will react to the allergen?

faq.a: Use a specific IgE blood test instead, as antihistamines suppress the skin response.
faq.q: What should be done if the patient cannot stop antihistamines before testing?

faq.a: Blood testing avoids the risk of provoking another systemic reaction during skin testing.
faq.q: Why is specific IgE sometimes preferred over SPT in patients with prior anaphylaxis?

exam: A 12‑year‑old with seasonal rhinitis and intermittent wheeze is referred for allergy testing. Which test is first‑line and why? — Skin prick test; it is quick, inexpensive, and gives immediate results for IgE‑mediated sensitisation.

During an SPT a patient develops sudden wheeze and hypotension. What is your immediate management? — Stop testing, call for help, administer intramuscular epinephrine, secure airway, give high‑flow oxygen.
A patient on chronic antihistamines needs allergy work‑up. How do you proceed? — Either stop antihistamines 5‑7 days before SPT or order serum specific IgE; the latter avoids withdrawal.

Explain why a 5‑mm wheal to dust mite but no symptoms after exposure does not require immunotherapy. — Sensitisation without clinical reactivity means no benefit; immunotherapy targets symptomatic allergy.

In a low‑resource clinic without SPT kits, what alternative confirms IgE‑mediated allergy? — Serum specific IgE assay (if laboratory available) or a detailed exposure‑symptom diary combined with therapeutic trial of antihistamines.

Differentiate between a positive SPT to peanuts and a false‑positive due to high total IgE. — Assess wheal size, compare with negative control, and correlate with clear history of reaction; high total IgE alone can enlarge wheals.
Why are first‑generation H1‑antihistamines avoided in a driver with allergic rhinitis? — They cause sedation and impaired psychomotor function, increasing road‑traffic risk.
List three common environmental allergens in East Africa that should be included in a standard SPT panel. — House dust mite, cockroach, grass pollens (e.g., Bermuda), and mould spores (Alternaria).
ai.title: Skin Prick Test
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The skin prick test (SPT) is an in‑office, minimally invasive method to demonstrate immediate‑type (IgE‑mediated) hypersensitivity to specific allergens. It guides diagnosis, avoidance strategies and selection of immunotherapy, especially where laboratory IgE testing is unavailable.

b: Positive test: wheal ≥3 mm larger than negative control after 15 min.
Negative control (saline) should be flat; a positive control (histamine) confirms skin reactivity.
sections.p: A skin prick test involves placing a drop of standardized allergen extract on the forearm or back and gently pricking the skin so the extract enters the superficial dermis. A wheal‑and‑flare reaction within 15‑20 minutes indicates IgE‑mediated sensitisation.

t.b: Does the patient have IgE‑mediated sensitisation to the suspected allergen? A wheal ≥3 mm indicates sensitisation; a flat response suggests no IgE to that allergen.
When is SPT unsafe or unavailable (e.g., severe eczema, antihistamine use, history of anaphylaxis)? A positive result confirms sensitisation; a negative result does not rule out clinical allergy.

b: Grade 1: Localised wheal/flare only.
Grade 2‑3: Systemic symptoms (urticaria, respiratory distress).
Grade 4: Anaphylaxis – airway, cardiovascular compromise.
sections.p: SPT does not grade clinical severity; it only shows sensitisation. Clinical severity is staged by the reaction pattern (local, systemic, anaphylaxis) using the World Allergy Organization (WAO) grading.

b: Environmental: house dust mite (Dermatophagoides spp.), cockroach, grass pollens, mould (Alternaria).
Food: peanuts, shellfish, tropical fruits (mango, papaya).
Insect venom: honey‑bee, wasp.
Drugs: penicillins, sulfonamides.
sections.p: IgE‑mediated allergy to inhalants, foods, venoms and drugs is common. In East Africa, the most frequent sensitising agents are house dust mite, cockroach, pollens, mould spores, and certain foods (peanuts, shellfish).

b: Seasonal rhinitis worsening during rainy months (mite proliferation).
Acute urticaria within minutes of eating peanuts.
Anaphylaxis after a bee sting.
sections.p: Patients present with recurrent wheeze, rhinitis, urticaria, or anaphylaxis after exposure to a specific trigger. History often reveals temporal association with seasons, foods, or insect stings.
SPT is the first‑line bedside test. When unavailable, serum specific IgE or total IgE can be used. A complete blood count with eosinophil count adds supportive information.

t.b: Is there IgE sensitisation to the suspected allergen? Positive wheal ≥3 mm confirms sensitisation.
When SPT cannot be performed (e.g., severe eczema, antihistamine use). Positive result confirms sensitisation; quantitative level may correlate with likelihood of clinical allergy.
Is there a background atopic tendency? Very high levels (>1000 IU/mL) suggest atopy but are non‑specific.
Is there eosinophilia supporting an allergic process? Eosinophils >0.5 × 10⁹/L raise suspicion for parasitic infection or allergic disease.

b: Rapid onset of wheeze, hypotension, or loss of consciousness during testing.
Persistent large wheal (>10 mm) with systemic symptoms.
sections.p: Although SPT is safe, severe systemic reactions can occur, especially in highly sensitised patients or with large allergen extracts.

b: Avoid identified allergens – the most effective primary measure.
H1‑antihistamines for intermittent urticaria; avoid sedating first‑generation agents when driving.
Inhaled corticosteroids for allergic asthma; add long‑acting β‑agonist if control inadequate.
Subcutaneous or sublingual allergen immunotherapy for mite or pollen sensitisation when avoidance is impractical; chosen because it induces tolerance.
Epinephrine auto‑injector for patients with a history of systemic reactions; avoid reliance on oral antihistamines in anaphylaxis.
sections.p: Treat the underlying allergy and educate on avoidance. Pharmacologic therapy targets symptoms; immunotherapy modifies disease course.

b: Repeat SPT or specific IgE when new symptoms appear.
Annual review of inhaler technique and trigger avoidance.
sections.p: Re‑test after 4‑6 weeks if antihistamines were stopped too early or if clinical picture changes. Counsel patients on proper storage of epinephrine and regular review of avoidance measures.

b: Non‑IgE mediated food allergy (e.g., FPIES) – no wheal on SPT.
Contact dermatitis – delayed (type IV) reaction, negative SPT.
Vasculitic urticaria – palpable purpura, not IgE driven.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic IgE‑mediated allergy but have different pathophysiology.

b: High background total IgE can produce false‑positive wheals.
Antihistamine use within 5‑7 days can suppress wheal size, yielding false‑negative results.
sections.p: A positive SPT indicates sensitisation, not necessarily clinical allergy; a negative test does not exclude non‑IgE mechanisms.

whenToSeekHelp: Anaphylaxis during or after testing (airway obstruction, hypotension, loss of consciousness).
Severe wheezing or bronchospasm unresponsive to inhaled bronchodilator.
